short: The cheap, mass-produced Soviet tank that ended up in forty armies.
full:
Adopted on 7 August 1973, the T-72 was the affordable alternative to the technically ambitious T-64: same 125 mm 2A46 smoothbore and carousel autoloader, but a conventional engine and running gear that could be built in quantity. Three crew, no loader, and a hull under 42 tonnes, roughly two-thirds the weight of its NATO contemporaries. Uralvagonzavod turned out more than 18,000 by 1990, with licensed production in Poland, Czechoslovakia, India, Iraq and Yugoslavia.

Export versions had thinner armour and older ammunition than Soviet ones, which is the main reason the Iraqi T-72s destroyed at Medina Ridge and 73 Easting in 1991 did so little damage in return. The carousel's exposed propellant charges give the family its characteristic turret-throwing explosion when penetrated, seen repeatedly in Ukraine since 2022, where both armies field it. The T-90 is a direct development, and the T-72B3 remains Russia's most numerous tank.
